title: The storm (Acts 27:1–26)
hookLine: fourteen days without sun or stars, and an angel: fear not
tomorrow: a ship about to break apart. why talk about breakfast?

lines: THE QUIET ONE KEEPS EVERYONE CALM.
NO SUN, NO STARS, NO HOPE.
cards: A group project goes sideways, and suddenly the quiet one is keeping everybody calm. Acts 27 has a stranger version. A ship bound for Italy, a wind called Euroclydon, and "neither sun nor stars in many days appeared."
The crew has thrown cargo overboard; Acts says "all hope that we should be saved was then taken away." The one who stands up with a pep talk isn't the captain. It's a prisoner, Paul.
Odder still: he says the same words twice in four verses. Be of good cheer. Why twice?

teach.h: I TOLD YOU SO, THEN GOOD CHEER.
teach.b: Start with the first time. Paul opens with something very human, a small I-told-you-so: you should have listened to me and not sailed from Crete.
Then: "And now I exhort you to be of good cheer: for there shall be no loss of any man's life among you, but of the ship." Big words from a man in chains. So he shows where they come from.
An angel stood by him that night and said, "Fear not, Paul."
Then the second time, and it's different: "Wherefore, sirs, be of good cheer: for I believe God, that it shall be even as it was told me." Here's the answer to the puzzle.
The first good cheer points at the outcome: nobody dies. The second points at the ground under it: I believe God. Nothing outside changes between the two.
The wind still howls. No sun, no stars.
Paul's good cheer isn't a weather report.
It rests on a promise, and he hands it to everyone on board, sailors, soldiers and prisoners alike. The storm still has days to run, until the fourteenth night.

how: Some Christians turn to the storm stories of the Bible in hard seasons, and some keep a short line from scripture, such as be of good cheer or fear not, to hold onto in prayer.

a storm Jesus calmed on the Sea of Galilee

p: the wind that drove the ship
the ground under the good cheer

s: Paul promised the ship would come through undamaged
no loss of any man's life among you, but of the ship. the ship would go.
Paul's good cheer came after the weather cleared
no sun, no stars, all hope gone. he said it in the middle.
Paul says be of good cheer twice in Acts 27
once with the promise, once with its ground: for I believe God.

games.q: a friend's family is in a long hard stretch with no end in sight. she asks you to just promise it'll be fine. what does Acts 27 suggest?
o: promise her the hard part will be over soon.
say the true thing you hold to, without faking the weather.
tell her cheer is pointless until things improve.
games.why: Paul didn't say the storm would stop. he said what he believed, and why, while it was still dark.

practice: Bring to mind a long storm, yours or someone's you love. Say the words out loud once, slowly: be of good cheer. Then hold them quietly through the sit, like a hand on a rope, and let the wind be what it is.

wordCard.voice: The storm. Days with no sun or stars, all hope gone, and a prisoner on his feet saying: be of good cheer.

orig.note: Greek: be of good cheer, take heart. Paul's word to the ship in Acts 27:25.

carryVoice: The line to keep: be of good cheer, said in the middle of the storm, not after it. See you tomorrow.
